topic: Third-party requests: who is the client
stem: The sporting director of a professional women's soccer club hires a consultant to work with Ifeoma, a striker in a long scoring slump. The director says the club is paying and expects a short weekly update on "what's going on in her head." Ifeoma has agreed to meet but has not yet had a session, and nothing has been settled about what the club will hear. What should the consultant do first?
options: Meet with the director and Ifeoma together to agree on roles and what, if anything, will be reported
Hold a first session with Ifeoma to learn her goals, then agree on an update format with the director
Agree on a brief update format with the director, then explain those reporting terms to Ifeoma at her first session
Have Ifeoma sign a release for weekly updates before her first session, since the club is funding the work
rationales: When an organization requests and pays for services for an individual, the Ethics Code expects the consultant to clarify at the outset who the client is, the consultant's role, and what information goes to whom. Settling this with both parties before any session protects Ifeoma's informed consent and the club's legitimate interests.

The right conversation at the wrong time: Ifeoma would start disclosing before she knows what might reach her employer, so the limits of confidentiality must be settled before the work begins, not after.

This settles the terms with the paying party alone and only informs Ifeoma afterward. She is the person whose information is at stake, so she needs to be part of the agreement rather than told about it.

A release is a consent tool, but signing an open-ended one because the club pays is not informed or freely given. Funding does not entitle the club to session content; the scope of sharing has to be negotiated first.
takeaway: When a third party requests and pays for services, settle who the client is, your role, and what will be shared, with everyone involved, before the work begins.

stem: A consultant is starting season-long group sessions with a university rowing team, where athletes will hear one another's comments. The head coach has agreed in writing to receive only attendance and general themes, never individual comments. At the first session, which statement about confidentiality is most appropriate for the consultant to make to the athletes?
options: "The coach hears only attendance and broad themes, and what's said in this room stays private unless someone's safety is at risk."
"The coach hears only attendance and broad themes; I'll keep comments private, but I can't vouch for teammates, and safety is an exception."
"The coach hears only attendance and broad themes; we'll set group privacy rules today, and I'll keep each of your comments between us."
"The coach hears only attendance and broad themes, and I'll pass on an individual concern when I believe it would help that athlete."
rationales: This covers the coach agreement and the safety exception but implies the room itself is private. In group work the consultant cannot guarantee teammates' discretion, and leaving that out promises more than can be delivered.

The Ethics Code calls for discussing the limits of confidentiality at the outset, which matters most in group and team work. This statement names what the coach receives, admits the consultant cannot control how teammates use what they hear, and flags the safety exception, so athletes can decide what to share.
Setting group norms is useful, but this statement omits the legal and safety limits on the consultant's own confidentiality and does not acknowledge that peers may still repeat things.
Well-meant, but it breaks the written agreement and makes confidentiality depend on the consultant's private judgment, which leaves athletes unable to predict what will reach the coach.
takeaway: In team work, state up front what goes to the coach, that peers' discretion can't be guaranteed, and the safety and legal limits.

topic: Informed consent and assent with minors
stem: Wen, a 14-year-old figure skater, is brought to a consultant by her father, who has already signed the consent form. At the first meeting, before the consultant has described the work, Wen sits with her arms crossed, says skating "is fine," and says she doesn't know why she is there. What should the consultant do next?
options: Spend the first few sessions building rapport around skating, and raise her agreement once she seems more at ease
Invite her father back into the room so Wen can hear his reasons and feel supported in taking part
Give Wen a short questionnaire about her skating goals so she can share her views in a less direct way
Describe in plain terms what the work involves and what stays private, and ask whether she wants to take part
rationales: Rapport matters, but assent belongs at the start of services. Delaying it means Wen takes part for several sessions without understanding or agreeing to what is happening.
Hearing a parent's reasons can be useful context, but doing it now adds pressure at the moment Wen's own voluntary agreement is in question, which undermines genuine assent.
Assessment is a later step in the consulting sequence. Starting it before Wen knows what the work involves or has agreed to it skips her assent.

Informed consent with a minor combines the guardian's permission with the minor's own assent. Explaining the services and the limits of confidentiality in age-appropriate language, then asking Wen whether she wants to take part, respects her autonomy and opens an honest conversation about her reluctance.
takeaway: With minors, get the guardian's permission and the young person's own informed assent before services begin.

stem: A consultant is assessing competitive anxiety in a youth soccer academy's under-12 squad. Several players arrived recently from Brazil and are more fluent in Portuguese than English. The consultant's usual questionnaire was developed and normed with English-speaking adult athletes, and it has a published Portuguese adult version. Which assessment approach is most appropriate?
options: Use measures validated for this age group and in each player's language, plus interviews and observation
Use the published Portuguese version of the usual questionnaire, plus interviews with an interpreter
Use a youth anxiety measure validated in English, and have a bilingual coach translate items as players answer
Rely on structured observation and coach ratings this season, and add questionnaires once players' English improves
rationales: The Ethics Code expects consultants to use instruments validated for the population and language being assessed and to draw on more than one method. Age- and language-appropriate measures, plus interviews (with an interpreter if needed) and observation, give a culturally responsive picture.
This solves the language problem but not the age problem: an adult instrument and its adult norms are not validated for 11- and 12-year-olds, so the scores cannot be interpreted with confidence.
The measure fits the age group, but on-the-spot translation creates an unvalidated version for the Portuguese-speaking players and puts a coach in the middle of their answers.
Observation is a valuable method, but this drops the players' own voice and delays assessment for the newer players instead of using measures validated in their language.
takeaway: Use assessments validated for the client's age, culture, and language, and combine methods rather than relying on one source.

topic: Assessment results and consent for use
stem: At the start of the season, a consultant gave a junior hockey team (players aged 18–20) a mental skills questionnaire, telling players the results were for their own development and would stay between each player and the consultant. Midseason, the general manager asks for each player's results to help decide roster cuts. How should the consultant respond?
options: Ask each player for written consent to release his results, and share those of players who agree
Give the manager general impressions of each player's mental skills without sharing the actual scores
Decline to share results, and tell the manager players may show him their own reports if they choose
Decline to share individual results, explaining the developmental terms players agreed to at testing
rationales: Consent sought midseason, with roster spots at stake, is not freely given, and a refusal would itself signal something to the manager. The original agreement should stand.
Translating scores into impressions still discloses individual assessment information for a purpose players never agreed to. Changing the format does not change the breach.

Leaving it to players sounds respectful of autonomy, but with roster spots at stake it pressures them to disclose, and anyone who declines is implicitly flagged. The developmental agreement should simply be honored.

Assessment data may be used only for the purposes clients consented to. Players were told results were developmental and private, so the consultant should decline and explain why; any future selection-related use would need a new, transparent agreement before data are collected.
takeaway: Assessment results can be used only for the purpose clients agreed to; a new use requires new, freely given consent.

stem: During an intake interview, Desmond, a 52-year-old masters cyclist, describes two months of low mood, loss of interest in riding and friends, poor sleep, and feeling worthless. When asked directly, he denies any thoughts of suicide. The consultant is not a licensed mental health professional. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Teach Desmond a cognitive restructuring routine for his self-critical thoughts while monitoring his mood
Share the concern with Desmond and recommend an evaluation with a licensed mental health professional
Give Desmond a depression screening questionnaire to confirm the concern before recommending further help
Complete the intake and set modest process goals, then revisit his mood at the next session
rationales: Cognitive techniques are part of mental skills work, but using them on what may be a depressive disorder amounts to treatment, which is outside the competence of a consultant who is not licensed.

Persistent low mood, loss of interest, sleep problems, and worthlessness are warning signs that call for clinical evaluation. Under the competence standard, the consultant recognizes the concern, explains it respectfully, and supports a referral; performance work can continue alongside treatment if appropriate.
The warning signs are already enough to act on. Screening to "confirm" delays the referral and edges toward clinical assessment the consultant is not trained to interpret.
Continuing the planned sequence is right for routine cases, but here it postpones attention to significant warning signs that goals are unlikely to resolve.
takeaway: Recognize the signs of a possible mental disorder and refer for a licensed evaluation; don't treat, screen to confirm, or wait.

stem: Halle, a 15-year-old swimmer at a club in the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement, tells the consultant during a session that her coach has been sending her sexual messages and touching her inappropriately after practice. She begs the consultant not to tell anyone. What should the consultant do?
options: Tell Halle this can't stay secret, then report it to the club's safeguarding officer to handle next steps
Tell Halle this can't stay secret, then contact her parents so the family can decide how to report it
Write down Halle's account in her own words and save copies of the messages before making a report
Tell Halle this can't stay secret, then report promptly to law enforcement or child protection and to SafeSport
rationales: Telling the club is part of following policy, but an internal report does not replace the consultant's own duty to report to child protection or law enforcement and to SafeSport.
Informing parents may follow, but mandatory reporting is the consultant's own duty and can't be handed to the family to decide; delay also leaves Halle exposed.
Gathering evidence is investigating, which is not the consultant's role. A report needs reasonable suspicion, not proof, and collecting explicit messages from a minor creates further problems.

Suspected abuse of a minor triggers mandatory reporting: the consultant is honest that it can't be kept secret, attends to Halle's safety, and reports promptly to law enforcement or child protective services and, because the club is in the Olympic and Paralympic movement, to the U.S. Center for SafeSport, following organizational policy.
takeaway: On a disclosure of abuse of a minor: don't promise secrecy or investigate; report promptly to authorities yourself and, in the Olympic movement, to the U.S. Center for SafeSport.

stem: Thiago, a professional golfer on a developmental tour, is short on money. He proposes paying the consultant nothing up front and instead giving her 5% of any prize money he wins this season. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept a reduced hourly fee plus a small bonus if he keeps his tour card this season
Accept the percentage, with a signed agreement that caps the total he could pay
Decline the percentage and offer a fixed fee, such as a reduced or sliding-scale rate
Waive fees this season in exchange for his permission to share his story in her marketing
rationales: A base fee lowers the share that is contingent but does not remove it; any bonus tied to his results creates the same conflict of interest.
A cap and a contract make the terms clearer, but the problem is the contingency itself, not how well it is documented.

The Ethics Code holds that fees are never contingent on a client's future achievement, because a stake in his winnings could bias the consultant's judgment toward short-term results. A fixed but affordable fee meets Thiago's financial need without that conflict.
This avoids a contingent fee but trades services for an endorsement from a current client, which raises the undue-influence concern behind the ban on testimonials.
takeaway: Never tie fees to a client's results; offer a fixed, possibly reduced, fee instead.

stem: Harriet recently earned the CMPC credential. She holds a master's degree in kinesiology and is not licensed in any profession. In her state, the title "psychologist" is restricted by law to licensed psychologists. She is designing business cards for her new practice. Which title line is most appropriate?
options: Sport Psychologist (CMPC), M.S. Kinesiology
Licensed Mental Performance Consultant, M.S. Kinesiology
Certified Sport Psychology Practitioner, M.S. Kinesiology
Certified Mental Performance Consultant, M.S. Kinesiology
rationales: Listing the certification does not cure an unlawful title. Her state restricts "psychologist" to licensed psychologists, and the word implies a licensure she does not hold.
The CMPC is not a license. Calling it one suggests state regulation and authority she does not have.
This renames the credential into something she was not certified as and blurs the line with licensed psychologists. The accurate approach is the credential's actual name.

The CMPC is a certification, and the Ethics Code requires accurate representation of credentials and compliance with local law on titles. Using the credential's actual name and her actual degree tells the public what she is qualified to offer.
takeaway: CMPC is a certification, not a license; use its actual name and follow local law on "psychologist."

stem: A consultant is launching a website for her practice. She plans to email her six current clients, a mix of athletes and business executives, asking each to write a short testimonial that she can post. What is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Drop the request to current clients and describe her services and training factually
Send the request, adding a clear statement that declining won't affect their services
Send the request, and post the testimonials with names and identifying details removed
Invite clients to post reviews on an independent review site rather than her own website
rationales: The Ethics Code does not allow testimonials from current clients, because their dependence on the relationship makes free refusal difficult. Accurate, factual descriptions of services, training, and credentials are the appropriate way to market a practice.
Reassurance helps, but current clients may still feel unable to refuse someone they depend on, which is why the Code rules out testimonials from them rather than relying on a disclaimer.
Anonymity protects identity but not freedom to refuse. The problem is seeking endorsements from people currently receiving services, not how they are labeled.
Moving the endorsement to another platform does not change who is being asked. Soliciting reviews from current clients carries the same undue-influence concern.
takeaway: Don't solicit testimonials or reviews from current clients; market with accurate, factual information.

stem: A consultant has worked with a university volleyball team for a year. Several athletes have told him in confidence about academic struggles and missed classes. The head coach now asks him to also take over academic monitoring: checking class attendance and reporting athletes who skip class so the coach can bench them. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept the role but report only attendance, never anything athletes have told him in sessions
Accept the role after telling athletes exactly what he will now report and to whom
Decline the role, explaining that reporting athletes for discipline conflicts with his work
Ask the athletes as a group whether they are comfortable with him taking on the role
rationales: Keeping session content out of reports is well-intended, but he would still be the person reporting athletes for punishment, which is the role conflict itself; athletes would reasonably stop confiding.
Transparency is better than secrecy, but it does not resolve the conflict. He would be policing the very behavior athletes have confided to him.

The Ethics Code asks consultants to avoid multiple relationships that risk impairing objectivity or harming clients. A disciplinary reporting role cannot be managed alongside the consulting role here: athletes have already confided academic problems to him, and the new role would turn that trust against them. Declining, and explaining why, protects both the athletes and the service.
Seeking their views sounds collaborative, but group agreement cannot remove a structural role conflict, and athletes may not feel free to object in front of teammates.
takeaway: Decline added roles, such as disciplinary reporting, that create a multiple relationship undercutting clients' trust.

stem: Tomás, a collegiate soccer player, asks the consultant to write him a daily meal plan with calorie and protein targets so he can add muscle during the off-season. The consultant took one undergraduate nutrition course, and the athletic department employs a sports dietitian. What should the consultant do?
options: Draft a starter plan from published sport-nutrition guidelines, and have the dietitian review it later
Share general fueling principles and connect Tomás with the department's registered dietitian
Ask the strength coach to set his calorie and protein targets, since the coach designs his lifting program
Help Tomás set goals for consistent eating habits, and leave the specific targets for him to research
rationales: Published guidelines are evidence-based, but turning them into an individualized plan with targets is nutrition prescription. Having it checked afterward reverses the right order.

A CMPC may share general, evidence-based information outside their core area but leaves individualized assessment and prescription to the right professional. Registered dietitians prescribe individualized nutrition plans, so connecting Tomás with one keeps the consultant within competence while supporting his goal.
Strength and conditioning coaches program physical training; individualized nutrition prescription belongs to the registered dietitian.
Habit goals are a legitimate mental skills contribution, but leaving targets to his own research skips the referral he needs for individualized advice.
takeaway: Share general information and support habits, but leave individualized nutrition prescription to the registered dietitian.

stem: Two consultants share a practice. Dana listens to her colleague's new podcast episode, in which he tells a detailed story about a "recent client," naming the client's college team, position, and injury. The episode is still public, and nobody else in the practice seems to have noticed. What should Dana do first?
options: Speak with her colleague directly and ask him to take the episode down
File a report with the AASP Ethics Committee, then let her colleague know she has done so
Raise it with the practice's other consultants so they can agree on a shared response to him
Contact the client's team to warn them that the story identifies one of their athletes
rationales: When confidentiality allows, the Ethics Code favors first attempting an informal resolution with the colleague. Speaking to him directly is also the quickest way to stop an ongoing breach; if he doesn't respond, Dana can consult a mentor and escalate to the AASP Ethics Committee.
Formal complaints fit when informal resolution fails or is unsuitable. Going to the committee first skips the step most likely to end the breach quickly.
Group input may feel safer, but it spreads the client's identifying details further and delays the direct conversation that could stop the breach today.
Dana has no relationship with this client or team. Contacting them would extend the disclosure and is not her role.
takeaway: For a colleague's ethical lapse, try informal resolution first when appropriate, then consult and escalate if needed.

stem: A consultant who holds the CMPC but is not a licensed mental health or health care provider begins working with a gymnastics club in the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement. Ana, age 13, wants to talk about her fear of a new skill. The only private room is a staff office at the end of a hallway out of sight of the gym. Ana's parent has approved the sessions. How should the consultant set up their individual meetings?
options: Meet in the office with the door left open, scheduled during practice hours
Meet in the office with the door closed, and log each session with the club's safeguarding officer
Meet at the edge of the gym, in view of other adults but out of their earshot
Hold sessions by video while Ana is at home, with her parent's approval on file
rationales: An open door helps only if someone can see in. This office is out of sight of the gym, so the meeting is neither observable nor readily interruptible by other adults.
Logging sessions creates a record, but it does not make the interaction observable or interruptible, which is the core MAAPP requirement.

MAAPP requires one-on-one interactions between an adult and a minor athlete to be observable and interruptible. Meeting in plain view of other adults, positioned so the conversation can't be overheard, meets that requirement while keeping reasonable privacy for Ana.
Moving online does not remove the requirement. A private video call with a minor alone is still an unobservable one-on-one interaction, and parental approval does not exempt it.
takeaway: Under MAAPP, one-on-one time with a minor athlete must be observable and interruptible, in person or online.

stem: Lorna, 61, took up running for her health and now wants help with race-day nerves. A freelance graphic designer, she can't afford ongoing sessions, so she offers to redesign the consultant's website in exchange for six sessions. If they agreed, the consultant would also be Lorna's customer, reviewing and approving her design work. What should the consultant do?
options: Decline, explaining that professional ethics standards do not permit bartering for services
Accept, and put the terms of the exchange in a signed written agreement
Weigh whether the exchange is fair and could strain the consulting work, then decide
Agree with Lorna on the value of the work, then accept if both of them find the trade fair
rationales: Barter is restricted, not banned outright, so this misstates the standard. Declining may still be the right outcome, but only after the risks are weighed.
A written agreement is useful but not sufficient. A signed contract can still describe an exploitative exchange or one that damages the consulting relationship.

Ethical standards allow barter only under strict conditions: it must not be exploitative and must not be likely to harm the professional relationship. Here the consultant should consider fairness and the risk that judging Lorna's design work could complicate the consulting before agreeing, or offer a reduced fee instead.
Settling a fair value together addresses exploitation only. It ignores whether becoming her customer, and judging her design work, could harm the consulting relationship.
takeaway: Barter is permitted only when it is neither exploitative nor likely to harm the consulting relationship, so weigh those risks first.

stem: A parent calls a consultant who holds the CMPC credential but no license. Her 16-year-old son, a pole vaulter, has been diagnosed with an anxiety disorder and sees a therapist. She asks, "Since you're certified, could you treat his anxiety disorder instead of his therapist?" What is the most accurate response?
options: "No; treating the disorder stays with his therapist, though I could offer coordinated performance work."
"Not instead of the therapist, but I could treat his competition anxiety while the therapist handles the rest."
"Yes, if his therapist agrees to supervise and the two of us coordinate his care."
"Possibly; it depends on whether his anxiety shows up mainly in competition or in daily life."
rationales: Educating consumers accurately about the credential is a professional responsibility. The CMPC certifies competence in mental performance consulting; it is not a license, so treating an anxiety disorder stays with the licensed clinician, while performance-skills work can complement therapy with consent.
Splitting the disorder by setting does not change what the work is: treating a diagnosed disorder, which requires a license the consultant lacks.
Coordination is good practice, but supervision by a licensed therapist does not make treatment by an unlicensed consultant appropriate. The disorder remains the therapist's to treat.
Where symptoms appear does not change the credential's scope. A diagnosed disorder calls for licensed treatment wherever it shows up.
takeaway: Explain the CMPC accurately: a mental performance certification, not a license to diagnose or treat mental disorders.

stem: A consultant's draft brochure for youth sport parents reads: "Proven to raise your child's performance by 20%—results guaranteed." The figure comes from one small study of college players' free-throw shooting. How should the consultant revise the brochure?
options: Remove the figure and the guarantee, and describe the services and research base in general terms
Keep the 20% figure, add a citation to the study, and note that individual results vary
Remove the guarantee, and state that the method improved free-throw accuracy by 20% in a study
Replace the claim with a quote from a parent describing their child's improvement
rationales: The Ethics Code's integrity standards require public statements to be accurate and not misleading. A guarantee and a figure stretched beyond its study misrepresent what mental skills training can do, so the brochure should describe services and evidence honestly.
A citation and a caveat don't make the claim accurate. One small study of college free throws can't support a 20% figure for children across sports.
This describes the study more precisely, but in a brochure for youth parents it still implies a size of benefit the evidence doesn't support for their children.
Swapping a statistic for a testimonial trades one problem for another; endorsements from clients' families raise undue-influence concerns and are not evidence.
takeaway: Advertise accurately: no guaranteed results and no claims that outrun the evidence.

stem: Three months after ending a successful consulting relationship, a consultant hears from her former client, Joaquin, an adult triathlete. He says he has developed feelings for her and asks to begin a romantic relationship. Both are single, and Joaquin points out that they no longer work together. What should the consultant do?
options: Accept after consulting a trusted colleague about the risks and documenting her reasoning
Decline, explaining that ethics standards bar this so soon after their work ended
Accept, provided she refers Joaquin to a colleague for any future consulting needs
Explore his feelings with him in a follow-up session to understand what they reflect
rationales: Consultation and documentation are sound habits in gray areas, but this isn't one; the Code's post-termination restriction is not something consultation can waive.

The AASP Ethics Code never permits a sexual or romantic relationship with a current client and bars one with a former client for at least two years after services end, because the power and closeness of the consulting relationship persist after termination. Three months is well short of that, so she declines whatever both people want.
Ruling out future work together addresses a later dual relationship, not the risk the rule targets: exploitation of a relationship that ended only recently.
Re-entering a professional role to process romantic feelings blurs the boundary further and can deepen the dependence the standard is meant to protect against.
takeaway: No romantic or sexual relationship with a current client, and none with a former client for at least two years after the work ends.

topic: Scope: return to play after injury
stem: Tamsin, a high school basketball player, is rehabbing a hamstring strain with the school's athletic trainer, who has not yet cleared her. She tells the consultant she feels mentally ready and asks him to tell her coach she can play on Friday. What should the consultant do?
options: Give her a psychological readiness questionnaire, and send the coach the results to support her return
Explain that return to play is the medical staff's decision, and offer to help her prepare mentally
Encourage her to tell the coach herself, since she knows best how ready she feels
Ask the strength coach to test her hamstring, then tell the coach whether she can play
rationales: A readiness measure can inform the team's picture, but sending it to the coach as support for playing treats it like clearance, which only the medical staff can give.

Injury evaluation and return-to-play clearance belong to the athletic trainer and physician. The consultant stays within scope by being clear about that, supporting her psychological readiness, and, with her consent, coordinating with the athletic trainer.
Supporting her voice is good, but this sidesteps the medical decision; the coach should hear about return to play from the athletic trainer, not from how ready she feels.
Strength and conditioning coaches program training; they don't make medical return-to-play decisions after injury.
takeaway: Return-to-play clearance is the medical team's call; the consultant supports psychological readiness.

stem: A consultant whose experience is entirely with team-sport athletes is invited to run a performance-anxiety program for a professional symphony orchestra, starting in four months. She has no training in the performing arts, where musicians face distinct demands such as auditions, playing-related injuries, and section dynamics. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept, and complete a performing-arts workshop during the program's first month
Accept, and use her usual athlete program, since performance-anxiety skills transfer across domains
Accept after building context knowledge and arranging consultation with a performing-arts expert
Decline, since mental performance services for musicians fall outside the CMPC's sport focus
rationales: The right kind of preparation at the wrong time: competence for a new population should be built before services begin, not while musicians are already relying on it.
Many skills do transfer, but an unadapted program ignores the context-specific demands that competent practice requires.

The Ethics Code's competence standard asks consultants to practice within their training and to extend it through education and consultation or supervision before taking on new populations. With four months to prepare, building context knowledge and arranging expert consultation lets her serve the orchestra responsibly.
Mental performance consulting extends to performers outside sport, including musicians. The issue here is her current competence, not the scope of the field.
takeaway: Before working with a new population, build competence through training and consultation rather than learning on the job.

stem: A consultant works with Ilya, a 16-year-old tennis player in a U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement program. Ilya asks whether he can text the consultant directly for quick pre-match reminders. How should the consultant handle electronic communication with him?
options: Copy a parent, guardian, or other responsible adult on messages, and keep them professional
Text him one-on-one, keeping messages brief and professional and saving a copy of each
Text him directly, and send his parent a brief monthly summary of what they discussed
Ask his parent to approve direct texting in writing, then keep messages professional
rationales: MAAPP permits electronic communication with minor athletes when it is professional in content and open and transparent, for example by copying the athlete's parent or guardian or another responsible adult. This lets the consultant support Ilya while meeting abuse-prevention requirements.
Professional content and saved records help, but MAAPP also requires communication with minors to be open and transparent at the time, which private one-to-one texting is not.
A summary keeps the parent informed after the fact, but the messages themselves remain private one-to-one contact rather than transparent communication.
Parental permission is not the same as transparency. The policy's safeguard is that another adult can see the communication, not that someone approved it in advance.
takeaway: Electronic contact with minor athletes must be professional and transparent, with a parent, guardian, or other responsible adult copied.

stem: Over three weeks, a consultant notices that Simone, a collegiate diver, has visibly lost weight, mentions skipping meals to "look right on the board," and has become withdrawn. Two teammates privately voice concern. The consultant is not a licensed clinician. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Raise the concerns with Simone, and add body-image and self-talk work to her sessions
Share the teammates' concerns with the coach, and ask the coach to talk with Simone
Raise the concerns privately with Simone, and refer her to the sports medicine team
Ask Simone to keep a food and mood log for two weeks so the pattern can be assessed
rationales: Talking with her is right, but treating possible disordered eating as a skills problem delays the medical and clinical assessment it needs.
The coach may need to know under protocol, but routing the conversation through the coach skips Simone and the referral to the professionals who assess eating concerns.

Weight loss, deliberate meal skipping tied to appearance, and withdrawal are warning signs of disordered eating and possible low energy availability. Within the competence standard, the consultant expresses concern directly and kindly and refers to the sports medicine team, which can involve a physician, dietitian, and licensed mental health professional under the institution's protocol.
Monitoring sounds systematic, but it delays care for warning signs that already justify referral and puts the consultant in an assessment role outside competence.
takeaway: Warning signs of disordered eating call for a caring conversation and prompt referral to the sports medicine team.

stem: A technology company invites a CMPC whose background is in sport to provide "executive coaching" to its leadership team. The request covers helping leaders perform under pressure and also advising on a major restructuring of the company's departments. She has no training in organizational design. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept the pressure work, and limit restructuring advice to its effects on leaders' stress
Accept the full contract under the title "executive coach," which carries no licensing requirement
Accept the pressure work, and recommend an organizational specialist for the restructuring
Decline the contract, since her mental performance training is built around athletes and coaches
rationales: Narrowing the topic sounds careful, but advising on a restructuring, even through a stress lens, is still organizational consulting she isn't trained for.
That the title is unregulated says nothing about her competence. She must practice within her training, whatever the role is called.

The competence standard asks her to offer only what her training supports. Performing under pressure fits her mental performance expertise; organizational restructuring does not, so recommending a qualified specialist for that part serves the client and keeps her within competence.
Skills such as managing pressure apply to executives and other performers. Declining everything overlooks work she is competent to do.
takeaway: In business settings, offer the mental performance work you're trained for and pass on the rest; an unregulated title is no license to stretch.

stem: A consultant reads a new study of 18 college basketball players reporting that a novel visualization method improved free-throw accuracy. An elite wheelchair tennis player she works with read about it and wants to replace her entire mental skills plan, which is working well, with this method. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Replace her plan with the method for a month, then compare her results with her previous plan
Add the method to her current plan, since it comes from a peer-reviewed study on imagery
Treat the finding as preliminary, weigh it with the wider evidence, and discuss fit with her
Look for replication studies, and set the method aside until larger trials confirm it
rationales: Trying it out feels empirical, but abandoning a plan that works on the strength of one small, distant study takes a real risk for very little evidence.
Peer review does not make one small study of a different sport and task strong evidence, and adding it now skips weighing its fit.

Evidence-based practice integrates research quality and relevance with practitioner expertise and the client's characteristics and preferences. One small study of a different task is preliminary, so the consultant places it within the broader evidence and talks honestly with the athlete about its fit before deciding.
Checking for replication is sensible, but setting the idea aside without discussing it ignores the athlete's preferences, which evidence-based practice also weighs.
takeaway: Weigh a new finding by its quality and relevance alongside the wider evidence and the client's needs; don't adopt or dismiss it wholesale.

stem: A consultant employed by a university athletic department is told by an administrator to save her session notes on the department's shared drive, which coaches and staff can also open. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Explain the confidentiality conflict, and work with the department on restricted-access storage
Comply, but keep the notes brief and free of sensitive details so little is exposed
Ask clients to consent to staff viewing their notes, as part of the department's intake forms
Keep her notes on her personal laptop, and give the shared drive attendance records only
rationales: Records must be kept securely and accessed only as clients have agreed. When an organization's demand conflicts with the Ethics Code, the consultant clarifies the conflict and works toward a solution consistent with the Code, such as storage that only she (and authorized clinical staff, if applicable) can open.
Minimizing content reduces harm but still places confidential records where coaches can read them, and thin notes weaken documentation.
Consent obtained as a condition of services, to suit the department, isn't freely given and doesn't address whether coaches should see the records at all.
This protects notes from coaches but creates a separate security and ownership problem, and it sidesteps the conversation the department needs to have.
takeaway: Keep records secure and access-restricted; when an organization's demand conflicts with the Code, raise it and work toward a compliant solution.

topic: Release of information to another provider
stem: Liam, a 27-year-old professional rugby player, sees a licensed counselor for grief and works with a consultant on performance. He asks the consultant to coordinate with his counselor so their work fits together. What should the consultant do before contacting the counselor?
options: Get Liam's verbal agreement, and note in his file that he approved the coordination
Ask the counselor to have Liam sign her release, then share what she needs to know
Have Liam sign the practice's general release, which covers any provider he names later
Have Liam sign a release naming the counselor, what will be shared, why, and for how long
rationales: Agreement and a note are a start, but a verbal okay doesn't define what may be shared or for how long; a specific written release protects Liam and both providers.
The counselor may need her own release, but it doesn't authorize the consultant's disclosures; each provider needs the client's permission for what they share.
A blanket release doesn't specify recipient, content, purpose, or duration, so Liam isn't giving informed consent to this particular exchange.

Coordinating with another provider requires the client's informed, written authorization. A sound release names who receives the information, what will be shared, why, and for how long, and Liam can revoke it, which keeps him in control of his information.
takeaway: Before talking with another provider, get a signed release specifying recipient, content, purpose, and duration.

stem: Nadia, a collegiate softball player recovering from knee surgery, tells the consultant she fears she will never trust her knee again. The consultant had the same surgery as a college athlete and considers mentioning it. Which approach to self-disclosure is most appropriate?
options: Hold off on disclosing until a later session, once their working alliance is better established
Mention the shared surgery briefly, then turn the focus back to Nadia's fears
Share the consultant's own recovery story in detail, then invite Nadia to compare it with her own
Describe the coping strategies the consultant used, so Nadia has a concrete model to follow
rationales: Timing matters, but there is no rule that disclosure must wait; a brief, client-focused mention now could support the alliance at the moment it is most relevant.

Self-disclosure is appropriate when it is brief, made for the client's benefit, and followed by a return to the client's concerns. Used this way, it can build trust and hope without blurring boundaries or centering the consultant.
A detailed story shifts attention to the consultant, and inviting comparison can leave Nadia feeling her recovery must match it.
Offering the consultant's coping as the model centers the consultant and skips exploring Nadia's own fears and resources.
takeaway: Self-disclose briefly and only for the client's benefit, then return the focus to the client.

stem: A consultant for a professional baseball organization is asked to sit in on contract meetings and share her impressions of players' "mental toughness." She recognizes an ethical problem, has reviewed the relevant Ethics Code standards and her contract, and is leaning toward one response. In structured ethical decision-making models, what should she do before acting?
options: Talk the dilemma through with a trusted colleague or mentor, without identifying players
Write out the likely consequences of each option, then act on the one causing the least harm
Explain her concern to the general manager, and ask how the organization would like to proceed
Ask the players as a group whether they would consent to her sharing general impressions
rationales: Structured decision-making models build in consultation with a trusted colleague or mentor before choosing a course of action. Discussing the dilemma without identifying players tests her reasoning, surfaces options and consequences she may have missed, and becomes part of a documented process.
Weighing consequences is part of the model, but doing it alone and acting skips the consultation step most likely to catch blind spots.
The organization will need to hear her position, but the general manager is a stakeholder in the outcome, not a neutral consultant on the ethics.
Consent matters, but asking players as a group, with contracts at stake, isn't voluntary informed consent and draws them into a problem she hasn't yet resolved.
takeaway: In an ethical dilemma, consult a trusted colleague or mentor (protecting identities) before acting, and document the process.

stem: A consultant is about to begin a first video session with Arjun, a firefighter who lives in another city. Arjun signed electronic consent and fee forms beforehand, which explained confidentiality and how sessions will run. Before starting the intake interview, what should the consultant do?
options: Confirm his identity and current location, a local emergency contact, and a backup phone number
Test the audio and video, agree on how to reconnect, and review the fee and cancellation policy
Review the limits of confidentiality, ask about his goals, and explain how sessions will run
Send him a crisis line number by chat, and suggest he keep it handy during their sessions
rationales: Technology-mediated services start with verifying the client's identity and setting up emergency preparedness: where he is for this session, a local emergency contact and resources, and a way to reach him if the connection drops. Without these, the consultant couldn't respond effectively to a crisis mid-session.
A reconnection plan is part of good setup, but this leaves out identity, his location, and local emergency resources, which are what make it possible to respond to a crisis.
These are normal opening steps, but the signed forms already covered them; what remote work adds before the intake is the identity and emergency setup.
Sharing crisis resources helps, but a generic number doesn't tell the consultant where Arjun is or how to reach help near him if a session goes wrong.
takeaway: At the start of remote services, verify identity and confirm the client's location, local emergency contacts, and a backup contact plan.

stem: A consultant plans to collect intake questionnaires, including injury history and a brief mental health screening, from 30 university athletes online. She is considering a free consumer survey tool whose default settings store responses unencrypted and let anyone with the link view the results. What is the most appropriate choice?
options: Use the free tool's password option, and tell athletes how their data will be stored
Use the free tool for the questionnaires, and collect the mental health screening on paper
Use the university's general online forms, and ask athletes to consent to the privacy risks
Use an encrypted, access-restricted platform, and tell athletes how their data will be stored
rationales: Transparency is good, but a password on a link doesn't fix unencrypted storage on a consumer service; the data still lack adequate protection.
Moving the screening off the tool protects the most sensitive part, but injury history is health information too and would still sit unencrypted and viewable by link.
Consent doesn't substitute for adequate safeguards; the consultant remains responsible for choosing a secure platform for health information.

Assessment data, especially health and mental health information, must be collected and stored securely. An encrypted platform with access limited to the consultant, plus clear information for athletes about storage and who can see their answers, meets both the confidentiality and informed-consent obligations of technology-based practice.
takeaway: Collect assessment data on secure, encrypted, access-restricted platforms, and tell clients how their data are handled.

stem: Before a consultant has met any of the players, a professional basketball team's performance staff sends him a spreadsheet of each player's sleep and heart-rate variability data from team-issued wearables, so he can "see who's stressed." The players were not told the data would go to a consultant. What should he do?
options: Ask the performance staff to tell players the data were shared, then begin using it
Set the data aside until players have been told about and agreed to his access
Use the data to plan general team workshops on sleep and stress rather than individual meetings
Review only the team averages for now, and look at individual data once he meets players
rationales: Telling players after the fact is notification, not consent. They still haven't agreed to a consultant using their data.

Using personal data in assessment requires the person's informed consent for that use. Setting the data aside until players understand and agree to the consultant's access, and clarifying the team's data-sharing policy, respects their autonomy and protects the trust he will need.
Team-level use feels less intrusive, but it is still drawing on individual data players never agreed to share with him.
Starting with averages delays individual use but still relies on data shared without players' knowledge, and meeting players isn't the same as getting their consent.
takeaway: Don't use athletes' app or wearable data without their informed consent to your access, whoever owns the device.

stem: A consultant leads weekly video sessions on handling pressure for a sales team whose members work from home in four countries. Members will discuss setbacks with clients and with one another. At the first session, which step best protects confidentiality?
options: Require cameras on, and ask whether anyone else is in the room at the start of each session
Agree on norms like private spaces and no recording, and note that discretion can't be guaranteed
Use a platform with end-to-end encryption, and tell members their sessions are secure
Have each member sign a confidentiality pledge, and explain that the pledge protects what they share
rationales: Cameras and a quick check help with presence, but they don't address recording, repeating others' stories, or the honest limits of confidentiality in a group.

In online group work the biggest risks come from members' settings and behavior, not the software. Agreeing on norms (a private space or headphones, no recording or screenshots, not repeating others' stories) and being honest that the consultant can't guarantee members' discretion sets realistic expectations and supports informed participation.
Encryption protects data in transit, but it can't stop members from talking or someone off-screen from listening; calling sessions "secure" overpromises.
A pledge can reinforce expectations, but presenting it as protection implies a guarantee the consultant can't give across four countries and home settings.
takeaway: Online groups need explicit privacy norms and an honest statement that members' confidentiality can't be guaranteed.

stem: Between video sessions, Camille, an elite fencer, uses the consultant's secure messaging app most nights after 11 p.m. to send long reflections on training, and she gets upset when replies don't come right away. The consultant never set expectations about messaging. What is the best next step?
options: Discuss with Camille what messaging is for, reply times, and what to do in an urgent case
Set an auto-reply stating her messaging hours, and answer messages within those hours
Reply briefly each night, and save her longer reflections to discuss at the next session
Suggest Camille keep a training journal instead, and explore it together in video sessions
rationales: Asynchronous messaging needs explicit agreements: what the channel is for, when the client can expect a reply, and that it isn't for emergencies (with the crisis resources to use instead). Setting these now, together, repairs the gap in the original informed consent.
Clear hours help, but a unilateral auto-reply doesn't explore what the messages are for or set a plan for urgent situations.
This is supportive, but nightly replies reinforce an unsustainable expectation and still leave the purpose and emergency plan undefined.
A journal can be useful, but redirecting her without discussing the messaging leaves expectations unclear and offers no plan for urgent needs.
takeaway: Set clear agreements for messaging between sessions: purpose, reply times, and what to do in an emergency.

stem: Midway through a video session, Corinne, a police officer, describes intense distress after a recent incident and says, "I don't see the point of any of it anymore." Then her video freezes and the call drops. She doesn't rejoin. At intake, the consultant recorded Corinne's location for sessions, the emergency services there, and a backup phone number. What should the consultant do?
options: Call the backup number, and if she doesn't answer, text her crisis line numbers to use tonight
Message her with crisis resources, and ask her to rejoin or call back as soon as she can
Call the backup number, and if she can't be reached, contact emergency services where she is
Call her department's peer support team, and ask them to check on her tonight
rationales: Trying the backup number is right, but if she can't be reached, a text puts the burden on someone who may be in crisis and doesn't confirm her safety.
Sharing resources is caring, but waiting for her to make contact leaves a possibly at-risk client without any check on her safety.

Possible risk plus a lost connection is what the emergency plan made at intake is for. The consultant tries the agreed backup contact right away and, if Corinne can't be reached and concern remains, contacts emergency services in her location using the information already gathered.
Peer support may help later, but it isn't part of the agreed emergency plan, discloses her situation to her workplace, and isn't an emergency response.
takeaway: If a remote session drops amid possible risk, use the backup contact and then emergency services where the client is located.

stem: At the end of the season, a consultant wants candid feedback on her work from a university lacrosse team and plans an online survey with ratings and open comments. The head coach asks to see the responses. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Collect responses anonymously, and give the coach the full set of written comments as submitted
Collect responses anonymously, and give the coach grouped results with identifying comments removed
Use a named survey so she can follow up, and share only summary results with the coach
Have the captains run the survey so it feels athlete-led, and pass the results to the coach
rationales: Anonymity is right, but on a small team detailed comments can identify their authors, so passing them on unedited undermines the protection athletes were promised.

Candid evaluation depends on athletes trusting that what they write can't be traced to them. On a small team, an anonymous survey, shared only as grouped results with any identifying comments removed (and athletes told this in advance), yields honest data while meeting the coach's legitimate interest.
Follow-up can be useful, but when athletes know their names are attached, they tend to soften criticism, which defeats the purpose of candid evaluation.
Athlete leadership sounds empowering, but routing answers through captains exposes responses to peers and removes privacy.
takeaway: For candid evaluation, collect feedback anonymously and share only grouped, de-identified results, as participants were told.

stem: Gustavo, a masters rower, has practiced slow-paced breathing daily for six weeks to manage pre-race nerves. His consumer wearable shows no change in his overnight heart-rate variability, but he reports feeling calmer before races, and his coach notes steadier starts. What conclusion is most appropriate when reviewing his progress?
options: The practice hasn't worked physiologically yet, so a different technique should be tried
His reports and the coach's notes agree, so the wearable data can be set aside
No conclusion is possible until the HRV reading changes, so judgment should wait
The HRV reading is one limited indicator to weigh alongside his reports and the coach's
rationales: Treating one consumer-device metric, measured overnight rather than before races, as decisive ignores converging evidence that the practice is helping.
Two sources agreeing is encouraging, but discarding the third throws away information that may become useful and overcorrects in the other direction.
Waiting on one indicator lets the weakest measure veto the others; evaluation weighs all available sources now.

Evaluation should triangulate multiple sources. Consumer wearable data have measurement limits, and overnight HRV may not reflect pre-race states, so the reading is best weighed alongside Gustavo's self-report and the coach's observations before deciding whether to continue or adjust.
takeaway: Treat app and wearable metrics as one limited source; triangulate with self-report, observation, and performance.

stem: A newly certified consultant wants to record her video sessions with a collegiate wrestler so she can review them with her mentor as part of her ongoing reflective practice. What should she do first?
options: Ask the wrestler's permission at the start of each session, and stop recording if he hesitates
Use the platform's encrypted recording feature, and delete each file after the mentor review
Get the wrestler's informed consent covering purpose, viewers, storage, and deletion
Have her mentor sign a confidentiality agreement covering the recordings before she starts
rationales: Asking is a start, but a quick verbal check doesn't give him the information needed to decide, such as who will watch and how files are kept.
Secure storage and deletion are good data hygiene, but they don't replace the client's informed consent to being recorded.

Recording sessions requires the client's informed consent: why the recording is made, who will see it, how it will be stored securely, and when it will be deleted, plus assurance that declining won't affect services. Reviewing recordings with a mentor is valuable once that consent is in place.
Binding the mentor protects the files once made, but the person whose consent is needed is the wrestler.
takeaway: Record sessions only with informed consent that covers purpose, viewers, secure storage, and deletion.

stem: Jae-won, a 22-year-old professional esports player and current client, sends a follow request to the consultant's personal Instagram account. The consultant's informed consent document doesn't mention social media. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept, and add a social media policy to the consent materials for clients going forward
Accept, and keep interactions to professional topics while the two of them work together
Leave the request pending, and raise it with Jae-won if he mentions it in a session
Decline the request, explain why, and add a social media policy to the consent materials
rationales: A policy is a good step, but accepting a personal connection first creates the social relationship the policy is meant to prevent.
Limiting interactions doesn't undo the personal connection, which still gives each person access to the other's private life.
Waiting avoids the connection but leaves the boundary unstated and may leave Jae-won confused or feeling ignored.

The Ethics Code's multiple-relationship standards apply online. Declining a personal connection, explaining the boundary in a friendly way, and adding a written social media policy to informed consent sets a clear, predictable boundary for current and future clients.
takeaway: Decline personal social media connections with clients, explain why, and put a social media policy in your consent materials.

stem: A consultant based in Colorado is contacted by Maja, a professional golfer who lives and trains in Sweden, about weekly video sessions. The consultant has never worked with a client outside the United States. Before agreeing, what should the consultant determine?
options: Whether Colorado's rules permit the services, since they will originate from a Colorado office
Whether the video platform meets both U.S. and European data-protection requirements
Whether the consultant's liability insurance covers sessions with clients living abroad
Whether the services and title used are permitted under Colorado's and Sweden's rules
rationales: Colorado's rules matter, but services delivered by technology are also subject to rules where the client is located.
Data protection is one piece of cross-border compliance, but it doesn't answer whether the services and professional title are permitted where each party is.
Insurance coverage is a sensible practical check, but it doesn't determine whether the practice itself is permitted in either location.

The Ethics Code expects consultants using technology to follow the laws and regulations where both they and the client are located. Before agreeing, the consultant confirms that the services and title are permitted in both places, including privacy rules, and plans for emergency resources in Sweden.
takeaway: For online work across borders, check the laws where both you and the client are located before starting.

stem: A star quarterback's emotional meltdown on the sideline goes viral. Followers of a consultant's professional social media account ask her to post her take on whether he has an anxiety disorder. She has never worked with him. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Post general information on performance pressure, using the quarterback's moment as the example
Reply that a licensed clinician would be better placed to answer, and suggest followers ask one
Post her view framed as possibilities rather than a diagnosis, with a clear disclaimer
Decline to comment on him, and offer general information about performance under pressure
rationales: General education is valuable, but anchoring it to his meltdown still invites readers to see it as commentary on his mental health.
Deferring to clinicians sounds humble, but it implies the question about this person is a fair one to answer, when no one who hasn't assessed him should speculate.
Hedging and a disclaimer don't make it acceptable to speculate publicly about a specific person she has never assessed.

Public statements should be accurate, within competence, and respectful of individuals' dignity. Declining to discuss a specific person's possible disorder, while offering general, evidence-based information about pressure, serves the public without speculating about someone she has never assessed.
takeaway: In public commentary, share general evidence-based information; don't speculate about a specific person's mental health.

stem: Abebe, a 24-year-old track athlete who currently works with a consultant, wins a national title. The consultant wants to post on her practice's marketing account: "So proud of my client Abebe for his win today!" Abebe's race result is public, but the consulting relationship is not. What should the consultant do?
options: Ask Abebe whether he's comfortable with the post, and publish it if he agrees
Congratulate him privately, and keep the consulting relationship off her practice account
Post the congratulations without the word "client," so it reads like a fan's message
Share the federation's results post, and add a short note praising his mental preparation
rationales: Asking respects his privacy, but a current client may not feel free to say no, and the post would still use his success to market her practice, the concern behind the ban on current-client testimonials.

The existence of the consulting relationship is itself confidential, and a public "my client" post on a marketing account also works as an endorsement built on a current client's success. Congratulating Abebe privately celebrates the win without disclosure or using him to market her services.
Coming from her practice's account, a congratulatory post still signals the relationship to followers, so dropping one word doesn't prevent the disclosure.
Praising his mental preparation from a consultant's account implies she is involved, which discloses the relationship as surely as naming him a client.
takeaway: Being someone's consultant is confidential; celebrate current clients' successes privately rather than in marketing posts.

stem: A consultant in private practice who is paid directly by clients and never bills insurance asks a colleague whether she can use a free consumer video app for sessions, since "HIPAA doesn't apply to me." Which response is most accurate?
options: HIPAA likely doesn't apply, so a free app is acceptable if clients consent to the privacy risks
HIPAA may not apply to her practice, but the Ethics Code still requires a secure, private platform
HIPAA likely applies to her as a provider, so she needs a business associate agreement with the app
HIPAA covers stored records rather than live video, so the app choice matters less than her notes
rationales: She may be right about HIPAA, but her confidentiality duty comes from the Ethics Code too, and consent doesn't replace choosing adequate safeguards.

HIPAA applies to covered entities (such as providers who conduct certain transactions electronically, like insurance billing) and their business associates, so whether it applies depends on her practice. Either way, the Ethics Code requires secure, confidential communication, so she should choose a secure, encrypted platform.
Self-pay practice without electronic billing transactions often falls outside HIPAA, so this rests on a mistaken premise, and an agreement alone doesn't make a consumer app secure.
HIPAA protects health information in many forms, including electronic transmissions, and the Code's confidentiality duty covers sessions as much as notes.
takeaway: Whether HIPAA applies depends on covered-entity status, but secure, confidential platforms are required regardless.
